title: CRLA/313/2004 of MADAN AND ANOTHER Vs STATE OF UTTARANCHAL

paras.text:
1
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND
AT NAINITAL
Criminal Appeal No. 313 of 2004
Madan & Another ..................Appellants

-Versus-State of Uttaranchal ....................Respondent
Present: Mr. R. S. Azad, learned counsel for the appellants.
Mr. J. S. Virk, learned Deputy Advocate General for the State of Uttarakhand.
Coram:-
Sri Sanjaya Kumar Mishra, J.
Sri Alok Kumar Verma, J.
Upon hearing the learned counsel for the parties, the Court
made the following order: (Per: Sri S.K. Mishra, J.)
1. The appellants, in this appeal, have assailed their
conviction and sentence recorded by the learned
Second Fast Track Court/Additional Sessions Judge,
Haridwar in Session Trial No. 388 of 1995 vide
judgment and order dated 04.09.2004, whereby the
appellants - Madan and Nathiram were directed to
undergo imprisonment for life and to pay a fine of Rs.
5,000/- each under Section 302 of IPC, 1860,
(hereinafter referred to as "the Penal Code" for brevity)
read with Section 34 of the Penal Code and to undergo

2
07 years imprisonment and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/-
each under Section 364 of IPC and also to undergo 05
years imprisonment and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/- each
under Section 201 of IPC with default stipulation.
2. The case of the prosecution, in short, is that
Dharmendra (Brother of the deceased) the informant,
PW - 1 presented a report before the SHO of the
concerned Police Station on 13.02.1995. According to
the informant on 11.02.1995 at about 03:00 pm, when
he along with his other relatives including his nephew
Pramod (son of Mahipal - deceased), his brother
Mahipal (deceased), Vijendra Singh, Ishwar Singh,
Karnapal, Surendra Singh and others were sitting
together, the accused Madan and Nathiram, who live in
Village Baleki came to our house and took Mahipal
along with them by saying that they have a Daawat for
Mahipal at Soni's residence, which is situated at their
village.
When his brother Mahipal did not return till 9:00 PM,
he - informant along with his nephew - Pramod went to
Soni's house where they found no one was present
there. When Mahipal did not return until next morning

3
i.e. 12.02.1995, they went in search of him in the
forest, where they heard from some of the villagers that
a body is found near the railway crossing of Ikbalpur.
When they reached there, they came to know that a
body was found on the railway track and it was taken
to Bhagwanpur Police Station and later on to Haridwar
for post-mortem examination. Therefore, they went to
identify the dead body and found it to be that of the
deceased and hence, a report was lodged. On the
registration of a Criminal case, the Investigating Officer
took up the investigation and after taking all necessary
steps for proper investigation submitted charge-sheet
against the two appellants for the aforesaid offences.
The prosecution took the plea of simple denial, in order
to prove its case, the prosecution has examined the 13
witnesses, PW 1 being the informant, PW 2 is one
Charan Singh, who speak about the last seen of the
deceased with the appellants, PW 4 - Pramod son of
Mahipal also speaks about the last seen along with PW
5 - Ashok Kumar.
Doctor S. S. Dhaundhiyal has conducted the post-mortem examination on the dead body of the deceased.

4
He found 14 ante mortem injuries on the body of the
deceased substantially as a consequence of crush body
parts including skull rib cage, legs, waist and cuts
around the chest, back, legs and waist. In the small
intestine - semi digested food material found with some
gases present and no abnormality detected and the
large intestine contains faecal matter and gases found
with no abnormality detected. He stated that death
could have been caused because of shock and
hemorrhage as a result of the ante-mortem injuries.
The doctor has not been examined in this case to give a
definite opinion regarding the definite cause of death as
he expired before he could be examined. PW 13 Veer
Singh has been examined to prove the post-mortem
report but he has not stated anything about the nature
of injuries and the cause of the death and whether it
was homicidal death or accidental death. The post
mortem report also does not reveal that the Doctor
came to the conclusions that it was a case of Homicide.
3. The prosecution relies upon the last seen theory in this
case i.e. stated to be by his son, nephew and the
complainant. PW1 Dharmendra has stated that Madan
was the nephew of Soni and the Nathiram was son of

5
Soni. Mahipal used to frequently visit Soni's house and
Soni was a widow. She had three children. In the
morning of 12.02.1995, Charan told him on
11.02.1995 at about 11:00 pm Madan, Nathiram and
Mahipal - Deceased were fighting in Soni's house and
Ashok told him, on the same night, he saw both the
accused Madan and Nathiram taking Mahipal on a
Chaarpai and when he asked what happened, they told
him Mahipal is not well and is under the influence of
Alcohol. He also stated that Mahipal used to drink and
also was not having any illicit relationship, but he
himself added that he had an alleged affair with Soni,
when Soni was 35 years of age. He further stated that
when they went to Soni's house on 11.02.1995 at
night, his son told no one is in Soni's house and did
not ask anyone regarding the whereabouts of Mahipal -
deceased, Madan and Nathiram.
4. The PW 2 Charan Singh has stated that on 11.02.1995
at about 11:00 pm, he was going to his fields to water
his crops and on the way to call his servant Karma,
whose house is situated beyond the house of Soni. He
saw Madan, Nathiram and Mahipal were abusing each
other and were involved in a fight, but he did not pay

6
much attention to the fight as they often had a quarrel
and fight after they consume alcohol, and therefore, he
went away. He did not inform anyone about the fight
that he witness between the accused & the deceased in
the night of 11.02.1995. He has stated that the
distance between his house and the house of Soni is
around 01 km and that he saw them fighting for two
minutes, but could not say. Why his statement was not
recorded by the Police in his diary statement.
5. PW 4 Pramod son of deceased - Mahipal stated that he
too was sitting with his uncle Dharmendra and the
deceased - Mahipal at that time when the accused -
Madan & Nathiram took Mahipal for a Daawat, about
3:00 pm on 11.02.1995. On the same night till 9:00
pm, his father did not return, he asked his uncle PW-1
to come along with him to Soni's house. Therefore,
they went Soni's house at about 10:00 pm, the gate of
the house was closed with a 'Kunda' on it. Neither he
asked from anyone regarding whereabouts of the
deceased and other nor he shouted for his father from
outside. On the next day, he heard, a dead body was
found near the railway crossing and Madan and
Nathiram had killed him. He admitted in the cross-

7
examination that Mahipal used to drink and he had no
idea, whether his father had illicit relationship with
Soni or not, but he used to frequently visit to Soni's
house.
6. PW 5 Ashok Kumar stated that on 11.02.1995 he was
going to Village Baleki from Ikbalpur on his scooter for
taking a tractor from Baleki Village. When he reached
near Baleki Village at 11:45 pm, he saw that Madan
and Nathiram taking Mahipal on a Chaarpai, when he
asked what happened, they told him, Mahipal -
deceased is not in a good condition and he is overdrunk
and due to which, he has become unconscious. With
the help of the headlight of the scooter he said that
both the accused had covered the face of Mahipal with
a cloth, which he neither asked them to take off nor he
took it off on his own. For about two minutes, he had
chat with them and could not see any blood stain on
Mahipal or Chaarpai. The witness has further stated
that they were moving towards in the direction of
Amarpur Village.
7. Basing on such evidence of last seen, the report of the
doctor, conducting the post-mortem examination,

8
recovery of weapon the instance of the accused person
and illicit relationship between Soni and Mahipal, the
learned Session Judge came to the conclusion that the
prosecution has proved its case beyond reasonable
doubt and proceeded to convict the appellants as stated
above. The appellants preferred an appeal before this
Court, which was heard by the Division Bench and as
per the judgment dated 07.09.2012, the Division Bench
held that the prosecution failed to prove its case
beyond reasonable doubt, and therefore, allowed the
appeal and set-aside the conviction.
8. The State took the matter to the Hon'ble Supreme
Court. As per the judgment and order dated
11.01.2018 in Criminal Appeal No. 71 of 2018, the
Hon'ble Supreme Court set-aside the order of the
Division Bench and remanded the matter for fresh
disposal, after rehearing of the matter. We heard the
learned counsel appearing for the parties at length, the
following are the evidences, which led the learned
Session Judge come to the conclusion that the
prosecution has proved its case beyond reasonable
doubts:-

9
i. The contents of the post-mortem report.
ii. The deceased was having an illicit relationship
with one Soni of Village Baleki.
iii. The appellants and the deceased were last seen
together on 11.02.1995 at about 11:00 pm and on
the next day, the dead body was found on the
railway track.
iv. The recovery of one axe and crowbar on the
discovery statement of the appellant - Nathiram,
which was found to be stain with human blood.
9. In a case of murder, when the prosecution alleges
that the accused person committed murder of
another individual, then it is the duty of the
prosecution to prove by cogent evidence that the
death of the deceased was homicidal in nature. If
there is any possibility that the deceased met with
an accidental death or that his death might have
been suicide, then the prosecution case cannot be
held to have been proved. The best way to prove the
fact that the death of the deceased was definitely
homicidal is to examine the doctor, who has

10
conducted the post- mortem examination. In this
case, the doctor, conducting the post -mortem, has
not been examined because he was died by the time
of the trial. The co-worker has been examined, who
has identified the handwriting of the doctor and has
proved the post mortem report to be in the hand of
the doctor S. S. Dhaundhiyal.
10. In any case, we have examined the post-mortem
examination report, the doctor has nowhere
mentioned whether the death was homicidal in
nature or not. All he has stated that the death of
the deceased was due to shock of hemorrhage,
because of ante-mortem crush injuries. Crush
injuries are in nature of injuries which can be
caused by the body coming in between two heavy
objects like that of wheels of a train and rails, on
which, it runs. The doctor has not specified if those
injuries could have been caused by the axe or
crowbar. In fact, doctor has also not been queried
by the Investigating Officer, whether the injuries,
found on the dead body of the deceased, could have

11
been caused by the weapon recovered at the
instance of accused - Nathiram.
11. In that view of the matter, there appears to be some
grey area regarding definite opinion regarding the
homicidal in nature of the death of the deceased.
However, if otherwise, the cases proved, then also,
the Court can come to its own inference and hold
that the deceased must have suffered a homicidal
death, and therefore, there is a need to examine the
other evidences available on record to find out if the
death of the deceased was homicidal and the
appellants are the author of the crime.
12. It is not disputed at this stage that 03 to 04
witnesses have stated that on 11.02.1995, the
deceased was called by both the appellants and
they went to Village Baleki. On 12.02.1995, around
noon time, the dead body was discovered on the
railway track.

12
13. Thus, there is a considerable time gap between the
last seen of the deceased alive in the company of
the appellants and the discovery of dead body.
14. In this connection, we take into consideration a
very recent judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court
in the case of "Surajdeo Mahto and Another Vs.
State of Bihar (2021) SCC Online SC 542", wherein
the Supreme Court has held that the case of the
prosecution based on last seen theory has to be
carefully applied and when the time interval
between the point of when the accused and the
deceased were last seen together, and when the
victim was found dead, is so small that the
possibility of any other person other than the
accused being the perpetrator of crime becomes
impossible.
15. The Hon'ble Supreme Court took into consideration
in an earlier judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme
Court in the case of "Satpal Vs. State of Haryana
(2012) 6 SCC 610", wherein the Supreme Court
held that the evidence of last seen alive may be a

13
weak kind of evidence by itself to found conviction
upon the same singularly. The Hon'ble Supreme
Court further held that it is coupled with other
circumstances such as the time when the deceased
was last seen with the accused, and the recovery of
the corpse being in very close proximity of time, the
accused, owes an explanation under Section 106 of
the Evidence Act with regard to the circumstances
under which death may have taken place. If the
accused offers no explanation, or furnishes a wrong
explanation, absconds, motive is established, and
there is corroborative evidence available inter alia in
the form of recovery or otherwise forming a chain of
circumstances leading to the only inference for guilt
of the accused, incompatible with any possible
hypothesis of innocence, conviction can be based
on the same. If there be any doubt or break in the
links of chain of circumstances, the benefit of doubt
must go to the accused. Each case will, therefore,
have to be examined on its own facts for invocation
of the doctrine.

14
16. In the aforesaid case of "Surajdeo Mahto and
Another Vs. State of Bihar" (supra) the Supreme
Court further held that the fact of last seen should
not be weighed in isolation or be segregated from
the other evidence led by the prosecution. The last
seen theory should rather be applied taking into
account the case of the prosecution in its entirety.
Hence, the Supreme Court further held that the
Courts have to not only consider the factum of last
seen, but also have to keep in mind the
circumstances that preceded and followed from the
point of the deceased being so last seen in the
presence of the accused. Applying that principles to
this case, this Court finds that not only there is a
time gap of more than 12 hours between the last
seen of the appellants with the deceased, but also
there is no other attending circumstances in view of
the fact that there is no motive has been
established, though, both the appellants are
relations of the lady Soni of Village Baleki, it cannot
be taken to be a motive because it is the case of the
prosecution in the sense that most of the witnesses
examined, who have stated that the Mahipal -

15
deceased was frequently go into Soni's house and
that he had relationship with her when she was 35
years of age. This Court is of the opinion that there
is no strong motive on the part of the appellant to
commit the murder of the deceased. Moreover, in a
case based entirely upon circumstantial evidence, it
is the duty of the prosecution to prove the motive.
The motive if not properly established by cogent
evidence, then it may weighed in favour of the
defence.
17. The only other material i.e. available is the recovery
of two weapons of offence i.e. axe and crowbar at
the behest of Nathiram, which was sent for
chemical examination. Though, the prosecution has
established that the weapon of offence were stained
with human blood, the blood group of both the
appellants as well as the deceased has not been
determined in this case. Therefore, it cannot be said
that the weapons of offence are definitely connected
to the commission of murder of the deceased. Such
would have been the case if blood group of
belonging to the deceased was found on the weapon

16
of offence. Moreover, in this case, the spot of
occurrence has not been verified or determined
objectively. A proper objective determination of the
spot, which would have lent credence on finding of
blood stains and their belonging to human origin.

18. In that view of the matter, in the ultimate analysis,
this Court is of the opinion that there are several
gaps in the circumstances relied on by the
Prosecution, and therefore, the complete chain of
circumstances has not been established unerringly
pointing to the guilt of the appellants.
19. In that view of the matter, the conviction recorded
by the learned Session Judge under Section 302,
364, 201 and 34 of IPC is erroneous and required
to be set-aside, hence, the appeal is allowed. The
conviction of the appellants and sentence awarded
to them by the learned Trial Judge are hereby set-aside.
20. It is stated at the bar that they are on bail by the
order passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court, hence,

17
they be set at liberty by cancelling the bail bond
executed by them before the learned Trial Judge.
21. Trial Court Records be sent back.
(Alok Kumar Verma, J.) (Sanjaya Kumar Mishra, J.)
02.11.2022
A/ -
